params.question: The three patients described — a man with triple-vessel coronary disease, a woman with calcified aortic stenosis, and a cyanotic baby — represent which three pathways of cardiac surgery?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Infective endocarditis and degenerative disease are real cardiac conditions, but they are not the three core surgical pathways described here. The three pathways map to the three cases: coronary blockage, valve disease, and a congenital defect.
Correct. Coronary artery disease (ischaemic), valve disease (valvular), and structural defects present from birth (congenital) are the three groups that define the scope of cardiac surgery.
Hypertension is a risk factor for ischaemic heart disease, not a separate surgical pathway. The first pathway is ischaemic heart disease caused by coronary artery narrowing.
Cardiomyopathy may occasionally require transplantation, but it is not one of the three core surgical pathways. The third pathway is congenital heart disease — structural defects present from birth.

overallFeedback.feedback: The three pathways are ischaemic (coronary artery disease), valvular (stenosis or regurgitation), and congenital (structural defects present from birth). This framework organises all the surgical concepts ahead.
Well done. Ischaemic, valvular, and congenital heart disease are the three pillars of cardiac surgery. Each has distinct presentations, investigations, and surgical approaches.

interactions.label: Medications can reverse a fixed coronary artery blockage, making surgical bypass

params.question: Medications can reverse a fixed coronary artery blockage, making surgical bypass unnecessary in most patients.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false. Coronary blockages, narrowed valves, and congenital defects are structural, mechanical problems. Medication manages symptoms but cannot physically reroute an artery, rebuild a valve, or close a hole. That is precisely why surgery is needed — it provides the structural correction that no tablet can achieve.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — the statement is false. A fixed coronary blockage is a mechanical obstruction. Medication can slow disease progression and manage symptoms such as angina, but it cannot physically reopen a blocked vessel. The same principle applies to stenotic valves and congenital defects: only a structural correction — bypass, valve repair or replacement, or defect closure — can solve a mechanical problem.

params.question: Which investigation definitively maps the site and severity of coronary artery narrowing to guide the decision between medical therapy, angioplasty, and bypass surgery?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An ECG detects rhythm disturbances and ischaemic changes but cannot show the anatomical location or severity of coronary blockages. It is a baseline test, not the definitive coronary investigation.

Echocardiography is the key investigation for valvular and congenital heart disease — it assesses valve function, chamber size, and defect anatomy. It does not directly visualise the coronary arteries.

Correct. A catheter delivers contrast dye directly into the coronary arteries, producing a map of exactly which vessels are narrowed and how severely. This anatomy then determines whether the patient is best managed medically, by percutaneous coronary intervention, or by surgical bypass.

Pulmonary function tests assess fitness for surgery and anaesthesia but provide no information about the coronary arteries. They form part of the overall pre-operative assessment, not the cardiac-specific workup.

overallFeedback.feedback: Coronary angiography is the definitive pre-operative test for coronary artery disease. A catheter delivers contrast dye into the coronary arteries, mapping which vessels are narrowed and how severely. For valvular and congenital disease, echocardiography fills the corresponding role.

Correct. Coronary angiography is the definitive test — it directly visualises coronary anatomy and guides the choice of treatment. Remember that echocardiography serves the same definitive role for valvular and congenital disease.

params.question: A patient with a mechanical aortic valve prosthesis is maintained on lifelong warfarin with a target INR of 2.5–3.5. What is the primary reason for this anticoagulation?

answers.text: To prevent the prosthetic valve from calcifying over time

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Calcification and degeneration are problems of bioprosthetic (tissue) valves, not mechanical ones. Mechanical valves are very durable and last decades; their limitation is thrombogenicity, not degeneration.

answers.text: To prevent clot formation on the mechanical valve surface

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Mechanical valve surfaces promote thrombus (clot) formation. Lifelong warfarin maintains an INR of approximately 2.5–3.5 to prevent thromboembolic complications such as stroke. This is the single most important distinction between mechanical and tissue valves — and the reason tissue valves are preferred in young women planning pregnancy, since warfarin is teratogenic.

answers.text: To reduce the risk of infective endocarditis on the prosthesis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Endocarditis prophylaxis uses antibiotics before certain procedures, not anticoagulation. Both mechanical and bioprosthetic valves carry a risk of endocarditis; warfarin does not protect against it.

answers.text: To improve haemodynamic flow through the prosthetic valve

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Warfarin has no effect on valve haemodynamics. Its sole purpose is to prevent thrombus formation on the mechanical valve surface. Haemodynamic performance depends on the valve design and size, not on anticoagulation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Mechanical valve surfaces promote clot formation, so lifelong warfarin (target INR 2.5–3.5) is mandatory. A bioprosthetic (tissue) valve avoids this need but degenerates over 10–15 years. That one distinction — mechanical versus tissue — drives lifelong management for every valve replacement patient.

Well done. Mechanical valves tend to form clots — hence the need for lifelong warfarin. This is also why tissue valves are preferred when anticoagulation is problematic, such as in young women planning pregnancy (warfarin is teratogenic).
